narrative.summary_main:
- **Retirement is the gap** — Your portfolio has to fund a long retirement while you keep saving from one salary. Your investable assets of $145,000 are a solid base. The clearest shortfall is that your savings and investments run out at age 85, leaving $32,439 of planned spending unpaid.
- **What the numbers mean** — Income covers about 34% of your yearly retirement spending need of $89,649, so savings must supply about $59,613 per year on average. Net cash flow is -$8,336 per year, so each dollar needs a clear job.
- **Where to start** — Rebuild your emergency reserve toward $46,530 to $55,836, and pay off the $3,500 credit card at 20% early. Then add to retirement: you defer $17,000 to your 401(k), so $7,500 is the most you can add. You could contribute up to $4,500 to a Roth IRA.
- **Order matters** — Retirement saving, cash building and card payoff compete for the same dollars while cash flow is negative, so we'll test the sequence. Cost basis in your taxable brokerage account is missing, so the tax effect of any sale isn't known yet.
- **Keep an eye on** — Your income depends on one employer, which adds risk on top of a thin cash cushion. Watch both as you build reserves.
narrative.snapshot_main: This snapshot covers the accounts we have on record for you: your 401(k), your HSA, your taxable brokerage account, and your checking and savings. Taken together, they form a portfolio built around a large taxable brokerage account alongside your retirement and cash accounts, with a thin cash cushion relative to the size of the investments.
narrative.portfolio_today_intro: Your portfolio is built for long-term growth, yet the same dollars also have to carry a retirement that currently runs short and keep a cash cushion that is still thin, so one pool of money is serving several jobs at once. Growth, safety and retirement income don't always pull in the same direction, which makes this a question of liquidity and sequencing more than of any single holding. The sections below look at how well today's portfolio serves each of those purposes.
narrative.portfolio_today_what_it_needs_to_do:
- **Safety cushion** — Your accessible cash of $30,000 covers about 2.9 months of expenses. A reserve of 5 to 6 months ($46,530 to $55,836) would let an unexpected event pass without forcing you to sell investments, which leaves you $16,530 short of the minimum. This money's job is to be available and stable, not to chase growth.
- **Retirement income** — Today's projection shows your funds lasting to age 85 and ending the plan $32,439 short, with a withdrawal rate of 5.59% at today's value. This is the long-horizon job, and it draws on the same dollars as your yearly cash flow and your cash cushion.
- **Long-term growth and tax-aware savings** — Your 401(k), HSA and taxable brokerage account carry the growth work, with $145,000 of investable assets. You defer $17,000 to the 401(k) with an employer match, and you could add up to $7,500 more to what you defer. You could also contribute up to $4,500 to a Roth IRA, with nothing contributed so far. Timing depends on how your cash flow allows.
narrative.portfolio_today_what_its_actually_doing:
- **Thin cash cushion** — Your accessible cash covers about 2.9 months of expenses, against a suggested 5 to 6 months ($46,530 to $55,836). That leaves you $16,530 short of the minimum. An unexpected bill or income interruption would likely be met by selling investments or borrowing, rather than from cash on hand.
- **Spending outruns income** — Your net cash flow is -$8,336 a year, which is 4.63% of gross income, after expenses, taxes and $11,400 a year of debt payments. Even though cash flow has improved from -$14,936, your day-to-day spending and debt service still draw on savings. That makes the cash shortfall slow to close on its own.
- **One employer carries both job and wealth** — Your $180,000 salary equals 82.38% of your $218,500 net worth. Your paycheck and most of your financial picture depend on the same employer. If that income were disrupted, you would feel it in your cash cushion and your investments' ability to keep growing at the same time, since the cushion is already thin.
- **Expensive debt sits beside the shortfall** — Your Amex card carries $3,500 at 20%, with $200 paid monthly. Interest at that rate runs well above what idle savings earn, so it adds to the pressure on cash flow. Your overall debt is $28,500, or 15.83% of gross income, with a debt-only DTI of 6.33%, which is modest.
narrative.portfolio_today_performance_timeline:
Over the three years to November 2026, your portfolio grew about 13.6% a year. A simple diversified portfolio holding the same share in stocks grew about 15.3% a year over the same stretch, so you trailed it by roughly 1.7 percentage points. Your value moved up and down by about 7.9% a year, against about 9.0% for that comparison. Per unit of risk taken, the two were close (1.27 for you, 1.30 for the comparison). In plain terms, you earned about what your mix of stocks, bonds and cash would be expected to earn. Three years is a fairly short record, so it describes this window and not a long-run pattern.

The most meaningful pattern is how you behaved in rough patches. In your worst stretch the portfolio fell about 10.2% from its peak and recovered in 62 days, while the comparison fell about 11.4%. You also fell less than the comparison in most market shocks. Around the April 2025 tariff pause, you fell 2.0% against 3.3%. Around the February 2026 Supreme Court tariff ruling, you fell 0.8% against 1.4%. The flip side is that you captured only about 72% of the market's gains in rising stretches, while taking about 91% of its losses. So you gave up somewhat more of the recoveries than you saved in the declines.

Your accounts differed. The 401(k) returned about 17.9% a year, while the HSA, which is mostly bonds and cash, returned about 3.0%. The paths of your portfolio and the comparison stayed close throughout, and the differences in individual shocks were small, so I wouldn't read a strong story into any single episode. Past results over this window are not a forecast.
narrative.portfolio_today_whats_working:
- **Employer match captured** — You contribute enough to your 401(k) to receive the employer contribution, which adds $7,000 a year to your retirement plan. That is compensation you already collect, and it builds alongside your own deferrals without any extra effort or cost from you.
- **Steady 401(k) deferrals** — You defer $17,000 a year into your traditional 401(k), against a $24,500 limit, and the account holds $80,000. Those contributions build tax-deferred retirement savings, and you are keeping them up alongside saving in your HSA and brokerage account.
- **Manageable debt** — Your debt-only debt-to-income ratio is 6.33%, with payments of $11,400 a year against $180,000 of gross income. Total debt is $28,500: $15,000 for the BMW 3 Series loan, $10,000 for the student loan and $3,500 on the Amex card.
- **Cash flow** — Your net cash flow is -$8,336 a year, leaving an annual gap.
- **Net worth** — Your net worth is $218,500.
narrative.portfolio_today_priorities:
- **Retirement depletion** — Your plan shows liquid assets running out at 85 and ending at -$32,439, with a 5.59% withdrawal rate at today's value. Closing that would take about $20,231 more per year, and those same dollars are also needed to cover your negative cash flow.
- **Thin cash cushion** — Your cash covers about 2.9 months of expenses, against a suggested 5 to 6 months ($46,530 to $55,836). That leaves you $16,530 short of the minimum, so an unexpected expense or income interruption could force you to sell investments instead.
- **Cash flow** — Net cash flow is -$8,336 a year, about 4.63% of gross income, even after improving from -$14,936. Spending and debt payments of $11,400 a year draw on savings, which limits how quickly the reserve and the retirement shortfall can both be addressed.
narrative.portfolio_today_verdict: You are doing real work in your retirement accounts: you defer $17,000 to your 401(k), your employer adds $7,000 a year, and your 401(k) returned 17.9% annualized over three years. The weak point is that this effort still falls short of the goal, with a projected shortfall of $1,177,586 and savings running out at age 85. Closing that gap would take about $20,231 more per year, yet your yearly cash flow is already negative, so retirement dollars compete with your 20% credit card, your emergency reserve and your January 2027 home purchase. Your 401(k) limit is $24,500, so the most you can add is $7,500 (worth about $1,800 in tax), and you could contribute up to $4,500 to a Roth IRA, where nothing has been contributed so far, though your eligibility at this income is still to be confirmed. What is at stake is a retirement income that lasts, and trying to do everything at once is likely to stall. You need a clear, paced path that settles which dollars go to the credit card, to cash and to retirement, and in what order, then reviews spending to fund the gap.
narrative.portfolio_today_also_meaningful: Your HSA is a smaller step to take after your larger priorities, such as the 20% credit card and building cash for your January 2027 goals. You have contributed $4,000 against a limit of $4,400. Adding the remaining $400 would save about $96 in tax per year, and it adds to a tax-free place to pay medical costs. Because your yearly cash flow is tight, add it only as money frees up. A second improvement is inside the account. Your HSA holds $1,500 in cash, $1,400 of it above a small working buffer, and that cash is earning 0.00%. Investing it inside the HSA, with no withdrawal, is worth about $104 per year on its own. Part of the $134 per year you could gain by investing idle cash in the HSA and 401(k) comes from this step. Your HSA's other holding is a bond fund of $3,500. Its payouts would cost about $38 a year in tax if held in a taxable account, and the HSA already shelters that cost, so it is not a saving still available to you. The HSA is mostly bonds and cash, and it returned 3.0% a year over three years. Reviewing the funds in the HSA for drag could help later.
narrative.recommendations_main:
- **Rebuild a liquidity cushion** — Your $30,000 of accessible cash covers about 3 months of essential expenses, against a recommended 5 to 6 months ($46,530 to $55,836). You are $16,530 short of the minimum. A larger buffer would let you handle a surprise without selling investments or leaning on the 20% credit card, which carries $3,500. You decide how fast to build it.

- **Confirm your January 2027 cash needs** — Your cash target is $163,330 to $172,636 once the $113,300 home purchase and $3,500 vacation due in January 2027 are included. Against that, you are about $133,330 short, and cash would cover 0 months afterward. Confirming the size and timing of those goals would show how much of the gap is real. It would also keep a market dip from forcing sales.

- **Make savings and cash flow fit together** — You save $43,000 a year, 23.9% of income. Even so, after taxes, spending and debt payments you run a $15,336 yearly shortfall. Retirement saving and cash building draw on the same dollars, so review spending and the savings mix together. Clearing the 20% card is a clear lever.

- **Close the retirement gap steadily** — Your plan shows savings running out at 85, with about $32,439 of planned spending unpaid, and about $20,231 more per year would close the gap. You defer $17,000 to your 401(k), so you could add up to $7,500 more, worth about $1,800 in tax. Your HSA has $4,000 contributed against a $4,400 limit. Any extra depends on what cash flow allows.

- **Look at where investment income is taxed** — You pay about $527 a year in tax on investment income, all in your brokerage account. About $247 comes from one high-yield bond fund taxed at 24%, which may fit better in a tax-sheltered account. The saving is modest, so weigh it against your other priorities.

- **Spread concentrated exposures** — Your $180,000 salary equals 82.4% of your net worth. Technology is about 33% of your stock holdings, and US holdings are about 85%. A downturn at your employer or in one industry could hit your pay and portfolio together. Review this against your growth goals.
narrative.recommendations_scenarios:
- **Pullbacks have been shallow** — Over the three years studied, your mix of about 59% stocks, 21% bonds and 20% cash-like holdings lost at most 10.21% from peak to low, and it recovered in 62 days. A diversified portfolio with the same overall stock share lost 11.44% at its worst. You earned 13.6% a year against 15.3% for that comparison, with smaller swings. Return per unit of risk was close: 1.27 against 1.30. These are past results, not a promise about future markets.

- **Recent shocks hit you a little less** — In the 90-day tariff pause rally (April 2025), you fell 1.98% while the comparison fell 3.27%. After the Supreme Court tariff ruling (February 2026), you fell 0.79% against 1.40%. After the final Fed rate hike (July 2023), you fell 4.19% against 4.63%. Your largest shortfalls were small: Operation Epic Fury was 0.29 percentage points worse, and the Liberation Day tariffs were 0.19 worse.

- **Recoveries were captured less fully** — In rising markets you kept about 72% of the gains of a comparable mix. In falling markets you took about 91% of the losses. So the cushion protected only part of the downside while giving up more of the recovery. This describes the mix you held over these three years, not a target mix, and it may not describe future markets.

rules: These facts are the only figures to quote for these concepts. Quote the label's meaning with the number; never relabel a fact as another one.
Each fact names the facts it must not be confused with. Never call one by the other's name.
Keep the unit: a USD/yr figure is always said per year, a lump sum never is.
Do not add, subtract or compare two facts unless a fact says how they relate.
Never quote a date that is before the plan date.
Write a date as month and year (August 2039), never as an ISO date (2039-08-01).
Write a ratio or rate as a percentage (55%), never as a decimal (0.551).

A fact's `replaces` lists key-metric fields that hold the same or a confusable figure under a misleading name. When you see one of those fields in your other inputs, quote the fact with its label instead. Field names are never labels.

spendingGap.note: Savings, cash and required IRA withdrawals included, pay this each year on average. It is what the plan asks of savings.
spendingGap.basis: today's dollars at the plan date
spendingGap.label: Yearly retirement spending that income does not cover, paid from savings
spendingGap.period: average over the 33 years of retirement

spendingNeed.note: Includes taxes, debt payments and goals after retirement; do not add those on top. annualTotalIncomeNeeded adds an estimated long-term care cost: do not quote it.
spendingNeed.basis: today's dollars at the plan date
spendingNeed.label: Yearly retirement spending need (excluding estimated long-term care)
spendingNeed.period: average over the 33 years of retirement

savingsRunOut.note: Never write a negative balance or a debt. Say when savings run out and how much planned spending would go unpaid. Net worth stays positive only because it includes the home.

savingsRunOut.label: Savings and investments run out at age 85
savingsRunOut.period: planned spending left unpaid by the end of the plan

savingsCapacity.note: It differs from net cash flow (-8336) because it subtracts the employer 401(k) match of 7000 as savings, though the employer pays it. Call it savings capacity, never spare or net cash flow. A negative value is a yearly shortfall: say it as one.
savingsCapacity.basis: today's dollars at the plan date
savingsCapacity.label: Savings capacity: after-tax income left after expenses, debt payments and current savings

guaranteedIncome.basis: today's dollars at the plan date
guaranteedIncome.label: Guaranteed income in retirement (Social Security, annuities, pensions)
guaranteedIncome.period: average over the 33 years of retirement; years before a benefit starts count as zero

incomeShareOfNeed.basis: today's dollars at the plan date
incomeShareOfNeed.label: Share of the yearly retirement spending need that income covers (guaranteed and other income)
incomeShareOfNeed.period: average over the 33 years of retirement

netCashFlowThisYear.note: The outflow table counts the employer 401(k) match of 7000 as household savings; the employer pays it, so this figure does not subtract it. Income 180000 minus outflows 195336 is -15336: never present that subtraction as this figure.
netCashFlowThisYear.basis: today's dollars at the plan date
netCashFlowThisYear.label: Net cash flow this year

averagePortfolioDraw.note: Counts only the months when spending exceeds every inflow. Required IRA withdrawals and other inflows drawn from savings are not in it, so savings pay more than this. Draws are concentrated in fewer years and are larger in those years. It is not the spending gap: never present it as filling that gap, and never use it to say the plan leans little on savings.

averagePortfolioDraw.label: Average yearly draw from savings in retirement
averagePortfolioDraw.period: average over the 33 years of retirement, counting years with no draw as zero

withdrawalRateAverage.note: A lifetime average. Do not compare it with the 4% sustainable rate.

events.description: The Fed raised rates 25bp to 5.25–5.50%, the 11th and final hike in the cycle — the highest level in 22 years. The Fed held here for 14 months before cutting in September 2024.
events.name: Fed final hike to 5.25–5.50%

events.description: Fed held rates steady but the dot plot signaled 75bp of cuts in 2024, marking a decisive pivot. S&P 500 surged to new highs; Russell 2000 +4%. Long-end yields fell sharply. Catalyzed a broad year-end rally across equities and bonds.
events.name: Fed pivot — December 2023 dot plot

events.description: Yen carry trade unwind and US recession fears triggered a global rout. Japan's TOPIX fell 12.3% — worst since 1987 Black Monday. VIX spiked above 65 intraday. S&P 500 fell ~3% at the open but recovered most losses by Friday. The episode lasted one week.
events.name: Global selloff — VIX spikes above 60

events.description: First Fed rate cut in four years, and an outsized 50bp move, formally marking the start of the easing cycle. Signaled the Fed's confidence that inflation was heading sustainably toward 2% and opened the door to subsequent cuts.
events.name: Fed first rate cut — 50bp

events.description: Trump defeated Kamala Harris decisively. S&P 500 surged 2.5%, Dow +3.6%, Russell 2000 +5.8%. The "Trump trade" lifted banks, small caps, and crypto on expectations of deregulation and tax cuts. USD strengthened sharply.
events.name: Trump election win

events.description: Chinese startup DeepSeek released an open-source AI model rivaling GPT-4 at a fraction of the cost, questioning the US AI capex thesis. Nvidia lost $589B in market value — the largest single-day loss for any stock in history. Nasdaq fell 3.1%, S&P 500 fell 1.5%.
events.name: DeepSeek AI shock

events.description: Trump announced sweeping reciprocal tariffs (10% baseline, 34% on China, 20% on EU, 46% on Vietnam) — the highest US tariff level since 1909. S&P 500 lost 10% in two days — the worst two-day loss in history ($6.6T erased). Long-end yields spiked on bond vigilante concerns.
events.name: Liberation Day tariffs announced

events.description: After the S&P 500 fell 10% in two days post-Liberation Day, Trump announced a 90-day pause on reciprocal tariffs above 10% for all countries except China (raised to 125%). S&P 500 surged 9.52% — its largest single-day gain since 2008. Nasdaq jumped 12.16%. Record 30B shares traded.
events.name: 90-day tariff pause rally

events.description: After two days of talks in Geneva, the US and China agreed to reduce reciprocal tariffs from 125% to 10% for 90 days. S&P 500 surged 3.3%, Nasdaq +4.4%. Apple and Amazon led gains as the deal eased supply-chain fears for import-dependent tech and retail sectors.
events.name: US-China Geneva tariff truce

events.description: The Supreme Court affirmed that the Trump administration's use of emergency powers to impose the April 2025 reciprocal tariffs was unlawful, formally unwinding the tariff regime's legal basis. (Exact date to verify on next run.)
events.name: Supreme Court strikes down Liberation Day tariffs

events.description: US and Israel launched coordinated airstrikes on Iranian military and nuclear sites, with nearly 900 strikes in the first 12 hours. Iranian leadership was decapitated. Brent crude surged 10–13% immediately; global equity markets sold off sharply on escalation and energy-supply fears.
events.name: Operation Epic Fury — US-Israel strikes on Iran

periods.portfolioExperience: Strongly positive: both equity and fixed income rallied, rewarding duration and risk after a painful Q3.

periods.portfolioExperience: Positive: equities and duration both rallied through the fall before the December hawkish cut capped the move.

periods.portfolioExperience: Positive for US-tilted portfolios, especially small-cap and value; international allocations lagged as USD strengthened.

periods.portfolioExperience: Negative turning strongly positive: V-shaped recovery rewarded investors who stayed allocated; international equities outperformed the full year.
